title: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume

slides.title: A Cuboid in 3D
slides.kicker: A rectangle that learned to stand up
bullets: A cuboid is the three-dimensional version of a rectangle, like the bricks and the Rubik's Cube pictured in the book.
It has six faces, and every single face is a rectangle.
Three numbers pin a cuboid down completely: length l, width w and height h.
slides.note: L, W, H yaad rakhoge toh poora chapter aasan hai.

slides.title: Surface Area From a Net
slides.kicker: Cut, fold, and count the faces
bullets: Cut out the net of a cuboid given at the end of the textbook, fold along the edges and join them to build the solid.
The faces come in three equal pairs, so each rectangular area gets counted twice.
Add all six faces and you get the total surface area: TSA = 2(wl + hl + hw).
slides.note: The net is just the cuboid lying flat before its folds.

slides.title: Volume Counts Unit Cubes
slides.kicker: How many little cubes fit inside?
bullets: Volume measures the amount of three-dimensional space an object occupies, in cubic units like cm^3 or m^3.
A unit cube measures 1 in every direction and its volume is set to one cubic unit.
The volume of a cuboid is the number of unit cubes that fit into it: V = lwh.
Picture thin l by w rectangles stacked like a pack of playing cards; each layer adds area of base worth of cubes.

slides.title: The Cube: Special Cuboid
slides.kicker: When l, w and h all agree
bullets: A cube is a cuboid whose length, width and height are the same; this common length is its side a.
So its total surface area is 6a^2 and its volume is a^3.
Both are special cases of 2(wl + hl + hw) and whl when w = h = l.
Volumes of cubes with sides 1, 2, 3 give the cube numbers 1, 8, 27.

slides.title: Right vs Oblique Cylinders
slides.kicker: Which way does the axis lean?
bullets: The word circular means the cross-section of the cylinder is a circle.
In a right circular cylinder the axis is perpendicular to the circular base; many pipes have this shape.
In an oblique circular cylinder the axis is inclined to the base; this chapter studies only the right one.

slides.title: Cross-Sections: Slicing Solids
slides.kicker: MRI scans slice you the same way
bullets: Take an extremely thin slice of a 3D object; the shape you get is called a cross-section.
Slice a cylinder parallel to its base and you get a circle; parallel to its axis and you get a rectangle.
When doctors take an MRI scan, they look inside your body in slices, just like cross-sections.
Cut fruits like a papaya or an apple and you see their cross-sections too.

slides.title: Unroll the Curved Surface
slides.kicker: A cylinder secretly holds a rectangle
bullets: Cut the curved surface of a cylinder as shown in the book and open it out: you get a rectangle.
One side of that rectangle is the circumference of the base, 2πr; the other side is the height h.
So the curved surface area is CSA = circumference × height = 2πrh.

slides.title: Tins and Tumblers
slides.kicker: Do the flat ends count? Depends!
bullets: A biscuit tin is closed at both ends, so the two flat circular ends add 2πr^2 to the area.
Total surface area of a closed cylinder = 2πrh + 2πr^2 = 2πr(h + r).
A tumbler is closed at one end and open at the other: surface area = 2πrh + πr^2 = πr(2h + r).

slides.title: Volume of a Cylinder
slides.kicker: Stack thin circular cards skyward
bullets: Like the cuboid, a cylinder's volume is the area of its base times its height.
The base is a circle of area πr^2, so V = πr^2h.
Same pack-of-cards idea as the cuboid, only the cards are round this time.
slides.note: Lallan ke pani vessel ka volume bhi isi se niklega, dekhna.

slides.title: Birth of a Cone
slides.kicker: Spin a right triangle, get a cone
bullets: A right circular cone is generated when a right triangle is rotated about one of its legs.
Three lengths matter: the radius r of the base, the height h and the slant length l.
They obey l^2 = h^2 + r^2, using the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem.

slides.title: Unroll Into a Sector
slides.kicker: Cut along a slant and open up
bullets: Cut the cone along a slant edge and open up the surface: it has the shape of a sector of a circle.
The radius of that sector is the slant length l of the cone.
Bring the two straight edges together and the cone forms again; try the net cutout at the end of the textbook.

items: You get a sector of radius l

slides.title: Why CSA = πrl
slides.kicker: Thin triangles add up beautifully
bullets: Cut the unrolled surface into a large number of very thin sectors; each one acts like a narrow isosceles triangle of height l.
Each thin triangle has area half of base times l, so the areas add up as half the sum of the bases times l.
All the little bases together make the circumference 2πr, so CSA = (1/2)(2πr)l = πrl.

items: Each acts like a triangle of height l

slides.title: Total Surface Area of a Cone
slides.kicker: Curved wrap plus flat base
bullets: The sector route agrees: sector area is πl × l × (θ/360), and matching arc lengths gives θ/360 = r/l, so CSA = πrl again.
The total surface area is the curved part plus the flat circular base: TSA = πrl + πr^2.

left.title: Curved part
items: unrolls into a sector of radius l

slides.title: One-Third of a Cylinder
slides.kicker: The famous factor of 3
bullets: Volume of a cone: V = (1/3)πr^2h, which is (1/3) × area of base × height.
A cone holds exactly one-third of a cylinder formed on the same circular base with the same height.
Students often wonder about the factor of 3; the book agrees this why deserves real thought.
slides.note: Ek base, ek height — phir bhi cone sirf teesra hissa.

slides.title: What Makes a Pyramid
slides.kicker: Every base point climbs to the apex
bullets: A pyramidal shape has a base that may be a triangle, a square or indeed any closed shape.
All points in the base are connected to a single point, the apex, which lies in a different plane.
You can make pyramids using the cutouts of nets given at the end of the textbook.

slides.title: Pyramids on Earth
slides.kicker: From Egypt to the Himalaya
bullets: The famous pyramids in Egypt have square bases.
A puzzle made by the Hungarian architect Erno Rubik has a pyramidal shape with a triangular base.
Some mountains have pyramidal peaks from glacier erosion over millennia: Shivling Peak in Uttarakhand and the Matterhorn in the Alps.

slides.title: Volume: One-Third Again
slides.kicker: Same formula as the cone
bullets: V = (1/3) × area of base × height, whatever the shape of the flat base.
The same formula applies for a triangular, square or any other shaped base.
It matches the cone because a cone is just a pyramid with a circular base.

slides.title: Surface Area: Just Add Faces
slides.kicker: No new formula needed
bullets: The surface area of a pyramidal shape is found by adding up the areas of all its polygonal faces.
That is why the book gives no separate formula for it: face-by-face addition does the job.

slides.title: The Sphere: 3D Circle
slides.kicker: Every point the same distance from O
bullets: A circle is the collection of all points in a plane at some given distance from some given point.
A sphere is the collection of all points in 3D space at distance r from a given point O, the centre; it is the 3D equivalent of a circle.
Rotate a circle about any diameter and you get a hollow sphere; volleyballs and footballs are familiar spheres.

left.title: Circle
items: points at distance r from centre

right.title: Sphere
items: points at distance r from centre O

slides.title: Archimedes' Wrapping Trick
slides.kicker: A tight jacket of a cylinder
bullets: Archimedes showed a sphere's surface area equals the CSA of a cylinder of radius r and height 2r that fits tightly over it.
That cylinder's CSA is 2πrh = 2πr × 2r = 4πr^2.
So the surface area of a sphere of radius r is exactly A = 4πr^2.

items: Fit a cylinder over the sphere

slides.title: Volume of a Sphere
slides.kicker: Four-thirds pi r cubed
bullets: Archimedes also found the volume of a sphere: V = (4/3)πr^3.
You will study the derivations of these formulas in later grades, using calculus.
A hint to try yourself: write V = (1/3) × (4πr^2) × r, that is one-third of surface area times radius.

slides.title: Mapping Earth on a Cylinder
slides.kicker: Wrap the world, unwrap the map
bullets: In cartography, a cylinder is tightly wrapped around the earth, touching it at the equator.
Radial lines from the north pole-south pole axis project the surface horizontally onto the cylinder.
Unwrap the cylinder and you get a rectangular world map, easy and convenient to use.
Defect: shapes are greatly distorted at high latitudes near the poles; near the equator the distortion is negligible.

slides.title: Solids All Around You
slides.kicker: Spot the shapes near you
bullets: Identify and list objects around you that are cubical, cuboidal, cylindrical, conical, spherical or pyramidal in shape.
Activity: find the approximate volumes of a gas cylinder, a bucket, a cupboard or a water tank near you.
Handy conversion for the activity: 1000 cm^3 = 1 litre.

slides.title: Guesstimates: Sensible Guessing
slides.kicker: Estimate when data is missing
bullets: Guesstimate questions ask you to make a reasonable estimate when exact data are not available.
You use assumptions, approximations, logic and everyday knowledge to model the situation.
The goal is a sensible estimate, not a perfectly accurate answer.

slides.title: Lallan's Golgappa Vessel
slides.kicker: Guess first, calculate next
bullets: Lallan's stall has a cylindrical vessel of radius 10 cm with pani up to a height of 50 cm.
Pani volume: V = area of base × height = π × 10 × 10 × 50 = 5000π cm^3.
Number of golgappas served = total pani in the vessel divided by volume of pani in each golgappa.
Before calculating, make a guess: is the answer in the hundreds, thousands, or more?

slides.title: Two Students, Two Estimates
slides.kicker: Both answers can be right
bullets: Student 1 assumed a golgappa radius of 1.5 cm and 60% pani: pani per golgappa about 8.5 cm^3, so about 1850 golgappas.
Student 2 assumed radius 1.75 cm and 80% pani: pani per golgappa about 18 cm^3, so about 870 golgappas.
Different but reasonable assumptions give different estimates; both calculations are sound guesstimates.

flashcards.front: Which three measurements describe a cuboid?
flashcards.back: Length, width and height, denoted l, w and h. All six faces are rectangles.

flashcards.front: Total surface area of a cuboid with length l, width w, height h?
flashcards.back: TSA = 2(wl + hl + hw): three pairs of equal rectangular faces, each counted twice.

flashcards.front: What does the volume of a solid measure?
flashcards.back: The amount of three-dimensional space it occupies, in cubic units like cm^3 or m^3.

flashcards.front: Volume of a cuboid in terms of l, w and h?
flashcards.back: V = lwh, the number of unit cubes that fit inside; the same as area of base times height.

flashcards.front: Surface area and volume of a cube of side a?
flashcards.back: TSA = 6a^2 and V = a^3, special cases of the cuboid formulas when w = h = l.

flashcards.front: What makes a cylinder a right circular cylinder?
flashcards.back: Circular: its cross-section is a circle. Right: its axis is perpendicular to the circular base.

flashcards.front: Curved surface area of a cylinder?
flashcards.back: CSA = circumference × height = 2πrh. Unrolled, the curved surface becomes a rectangle.

flashcards.front: TSA of a cylinder closed at both ends, like a biscuit tin?
flashcards.back: TSA = 2πrh + 2πr^2 = 2πr(h + r). The two circular ends together add 2πr^2.

flashcards.front: Cross-section of a cylinder sliced parallel to its axis?
flashcards.back: A rectangle. A slice parallel to the base gives a circle instead.

flashcards.front: How is a right circular cone generated?
flashcards.back: By rotating a right triangle about one of its legs.

flashcards.front: Relation between slant l, height h and radius r of a cone?
flashcards.back: l^2 = h^2 + r^2, from the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem.

flashcards.front: Curved surface area of a cone?
flashcards.back: CSA = πrl. The unrolled cone is a sector; its thin triangles sum to half the base circumference times l.

flashcards.front: Total surface area of a cone?
flashcards.back: TSA = πrl + πr^2: the curved portion plus the flat circular base.

flashcards.front: Volume of a cone with radius r and height h?
flashcards.back: V = (1/3)πr^2h, exactly one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height.

flashcards.front: Volume of any pyramidal shape?
flashcards.back: V = (1/3) × area of base × height, whether the base is triangular, square or any flat shape.

flashcards.front: How do you find the surface area of a pyramid?
flashcards.back: Add the areas of all the polygonal faces; no separate formula is needed.

flashcards.front: Name two real mountains with pyramidal peaks.
flashcards.back: Shivling Peak in Uttarakhand, India, and the Matterhorn in the Alps, shaped by glacier erosion.

flashcards.front: Define a sphere.
flashcards.back: All points in 3D space at a given distance r from a centre O; the 3D equivalent of a circle.

flashcards.front: Surface area of a sphere of radius r?
flashcards.back: A = 4πr^2, shown by Archimedes using a tight-fitting cylinder.

flashcards.front: Volume of a sphere of radius r?
flashcards.back: V = (4/3)πr^3. Its full derivation waits for calculus in later grades.

flashcards.front: Which cylinder's curved area equals a sphere's surface area?
flashcards.back: A cylinder of radius r and height 2r that fits tightly over the sphere: 2πrh = 4πr^2.

flashcards.front: What is a guesstimate?
flashcards.back: A reasonable estimate made using assumptions, approximations, logic and everyday knowledge when exact data are unavailable.

flashcards.front: How many cubic centimetres make one litre?
flashcards.back: 1000 cm^3 = 1 litre, the conversion used for buckets, tanks and vessels.

flashcards.front: Roughly how many golgappas can Lallan's pani vessel serve?
flashcards.back: About 1850 or about 870, depending on the assumed golgappa radius and pani fill; both are fair guesstimates.

quiz.q: How many faces does a cuboid have?
quiz.why: All six faces are rectangles; the net shows three equal pairs.

quiz.q: A cube has side 3 cm. What is its volume?
quiz.why: V = a^3 = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27; choosing 9 means you squared instead of cubed.

quiz.q: A cuboid has l = 5 cm, w = 3 cm, h = 2 cm. Its total surface area is:
quiz.why: TSA = 2(wl + hl + hw) = 2(15 + 10 + 6) = 62; 31 forgets to double the pairs.

quiz.q: Why is the volume of a cuboid also written as area of base × height?
options: Because a cuboid is like many thin base rectangles stacked, one per unit height
Because height always equals width in a cuboid
Because area and volume measure the same thing
Because the base of a cuboid is always a square
quiz.why: The book stacks thin l by w pieces like playing cards; each layer adds lw per unit height.

quiz.q: The curved surface area of a right circular cylinder is:
quiz.why: Unrolled it is a rectangle: circumference 2πr times height h.

quiz.q: A very thin slice of a cylinder is taken parallel to its base. The cross-section is a:
quiz.why: Parallel to the base gives a circle; parallel to the axis gives a rectangle.

quiz.q: A closed cylindrical tin has r = 7 cm and h = 10 cm. Its TSA is:
quiz.why: TSA = 2πr(h + r) = 2π × 7 × 17 = 238π; 140π forgets the two ends.

quiz.q: A tumbler (closed at one end, open at the other) has r = 5 cm, h = 14 cm. Its surface area is:
quiz.why: One end only: 2πrh + πr^2 = 140π + 25π = 165π; 190π wrongly closes both ends.

quiz.q: Rotating a right triangle about one of its legs generates a:
quiz.why: The book generates the right circular cone exactly this way.

quiz.q: A cone has base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. Its slant length l is:
quiz.why: l^2 = h^2 + r^2 = 16 + 9 = 25 by Baudhāyana-Pythagoras, so l = 5; 7 adds instead of squaring.

quiz.q: A cone's volume is what fraction of a cylinder with the same base and height?
quiz.why: V = (1/3)πr^2h, exactly one-third of the matching cylinder.

quiz.q: Why does the cone's curved surface area come out as πrl?
options: Because it equals the area of the circular base
Because it unrolls exactly like a cylinder
Because l always equals r in a cone
Because thin unrolled triangles sum to half the base circumference times l
quiz.why: Each thin sector acts like an isosceles triangle of height l; the sum is (1/2)(2πr)l = πrl.

quiz.q: A pyramid has a square base of side 6 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is:
quiz.why: V = (1/3) × base area × height = (1/3) × 36 × 10 = 120; 360 forgets the one-third.

quiz.q: A cone can be thought of as a pyramid with which base?
quiz.why: The book says a cone is a pyramid with a circular base; their volume formulas match.

quiz.q: Shivling Peak and the Matterhorn have pyramidal peaks formed by:
quiz.why: The book credits glacier erosion over many millennia for these pyramidal peaks.

quiz.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius r is:
quiz.why: Archimedes matched it to the CSA 2πrh of a tight cylinder with h = 2r, giving 4πr^2.

quiz.q: The volume of a sphere of radius 3 cm is:
quiz.why: V = (4/3)πr^3 = (4/3) × 27π = 36π; 27π drops the factor 4/3.

quiz.q: In a rectangular map projection of the earth, shape distortion is greatest:
quiz.why: The book notes great distortion at high latitudes; near the equator it is negligible.

quiz.q: The sphere's volume can be written as one-third of its surface area times:
quiz.why: V = (1/3) × (4πr^2) × r, so volume of sphere = one-third × surface area × radius.

quiz.q: How many cubic centimetres make one litre?
quiz.why: The book's activity uses 1000 cm^3 = 1 litre for buckets and tanks.

quiz.q: Lallan's vessel has radius 10 cm with pani up to height 50 cm. The pani volume is:
quiz.why: V = area of base × height = π × 10 × 10 × 50 = 5000π cm^3.

quiz.q: Two students got about 1850 and about 870 golgappas from the same vessel. The main reason is:
options: One of them computed the vessel volume wrongly
Only one of them used the sphere formula
The vessel shrank between the two calculations
They assumed different golgappa radii and pani fill levels
quiz.why: Student 1 took radius 1.5 cm and 60% pani, Student 2 took 1.75 cm and 80%, so the estimates differ.

examples.title: TSA and volume of a cuboid
examples.problem: A cuboid brick has length 10 cm, width 6 cm and height 4 cm. Find its total surface area and its volume.
steps: List the dimensions: l = 10 cm, w = 6 cm, h = 4 cm.
Add inside the bracket: 60 + 40 + 24 = 124, then double: TSA = 248 cm^2.
Volume V = lwh = 10 × 6 × 4 = 240 cm^3, so 240 unit cubes of side 1 cm fit inside.

examples.title: A closed biscuit-tin cylinder
examples.problem: A biscuit tin is a cylinder closed at both ends, with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Find its total surface area and its volume.
steps: The two circular ends add 2πr^2 = 2π × 49 = 98π cm^2.
Volume V = area of base × height = πr^2h = π × 49 × 10 = 490π cm^3, about 1539.4 cm^3.
examples.answer: TSA = 238π cm^2 (about 747.7 cm^2) and V = 490π cm^3 (about 1539.4 cm^3).

examples.title: A cone from a 3-4-5 triangle
examples.problem: A right circular cone has base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. Find its slant length, CSA, TSA and volume.
steps: Slant length: l^2 = h^2 + r^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 25, so l = 5 cm (Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem).
Volume V = (1/3)πr^2h = (1/3) × π × 9 × 4 = 12π cm^3, one-third of the matching cylinder's 36π cm^3.
examples.answer: l = 5 cm, CSA = 15π cm^2, TSA = 24π cm^2 and V = 12π cm^3.

examples.title: Lallan's golgappa guesstimate
examples.problem: Lallan's stall has a cylindrical vessel of radius 10 cm with pani up to a height of 50 cm. Estimate how many spherical golgappas he can serve, assuming each golgappa has radius 1.5 cm and holds 60% pani on average.
steps: Pani in the vessel: V = area of base × height = π × 10 × 10 × 50 = 5000π cm^3.
Volume of one golgappa: (4/3) × π × 1.5^3 ≈ 14.14 cm^3, neglecting its thickness.
Number served = total pani ÷ pani per golgappa = 5000π ÷ 8.5 ≈ 1848.
examples.answer: Lallan can serve about 1850 golgappas. Student 2's assumptions (radius 1.75 cm, 80% pani) give about 870; both are reasonable guesstimates.

steps.label: Start with rectangles
steps.detail: A cuboid is a 3D rectangle with length l, width w, height h.

steps.label: Box it up
steps.detail: TSA = 2(wl + hl + hw) from the net; V = lwh by counting unit cubes.

steps.label: Spin a cylinder
steps.detail: Unroll the curved surface into a rectangle: CSA = 2πrh; volume = πr^2h.

steps.label: Slice cross-sections
steps.detail: Parallel to base gives a circle, parallel to axis gives a rectangle.

steps.label: Unroll cone sectors
steps.detail: l^2 = h^2 + r^2, CSA = πrl, volume exactly one-third of the cylinder.

steps.label: Point the pyramid
steps.detail: Any flat base to an apex; V = (1/3) × base area × height.

steps.label: Wrap the sphere
steps.detail: Archimedes: area 4πr^2 via a tight cylinder; volume (4/3)πr^3.

steps.label: Guesstimate around you
steps.detail: Use the formulas with assumptions, like counting Lallan's golgappas.
